The distance to IRC -10414 was re-estimated on the basis of the statistical treatment of parallax and the model-fitting method, yielding <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$D=$</tex> 3.1<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\pm$</tex>0.4kpc and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$D=$</tex> 2.0<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\pm$</tex>0.2kpc, respectively. The estimated distance, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$D=$</tex> 2-3kpc, is much larger than that previously adopted. The stellar luminosity of IRC -10414 is also re-estimated to be <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$L_{\ast}\sim 9\times10^{4}$</tex>(<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$D/$</tex>2kpc)<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{2} L_{\odot}$</tex>, much brighter by a factor of 10-20 than previously adopted (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$L_{\ast} \sim 10000L_{\odot}$</tex>). The maser motions exhibit not only a spherically expanding flow with a velocity of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex> 10(<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$D/$</tex>2kpc)kms<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>, but also a faster bipolar outflow with a major axis in the north-south direction and at a small inclination angle with respect to the celestial sphere. These characteristics of the star and the circumstellar envelope seen in IRC -10414 are very similar to those in some supergiants exhibiting bipolar stellar mass loss.

articleTitle: Multiple-Component Analysis of the Time-Resolved Spectra of GRB041006: A Clue to the Nature of the Underlying Soft Component of GRBs
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: GRB041006 was detected by HETE-2 on 2004 October 06. The light curves in four different energy bands display different features. At higher energy bands several peaks are seen in the light curve, while at lower energy bands a single broader bump dominates. It is expected that these different features are the result of a mixture of several components, each of which has different energetics and variability. We analyzed the time-resolved spectra, which were resolved into several components. These components can be classified into two distinct classes. One is a component that has an exponential decay of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$E_{\rm p}$</tex> with a characteristic timescale shorter than <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim\;$</tex>30 s; its spectrum is well represented by a broken power-law function, which is frequently observed in many prompt GRB emissions, so it should have an internal-shock origin. Another is a component whose <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$E_{\rm p}$</tex> is almost unchanged with a characteristic timescale longer than <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim\;$</tex>60 s, and shows a very soft emission and slower variability. The spectrum is characterized by either a broken power law or a black-body spectrum. By assuming that the soft component is a thermal emission, the radiation radius is initially <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$4.4 \times 10^{6}$</tex>km, which is a typical radius of a blue supergiant, and its expansion velocity is <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$2.4 \times 10^{5}$</tex>km s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex> in the source frame.

articleTitle: Statistical Properties of Stellar HO Masers− Results of Three−Year Single−Dish Observations with the VERA Iriki Telescope
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We report on the results of monitoring observations of 242 stellar H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$_2$</tex>O masers, which have been made with the Iriki 20m telescope of the VLBI Exploration of Radio Astrometry (VERA) from 2003 July to 2006 November. The present paper mainly focuses on 85 stellar H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$_2$</tex>O masers that have been tightly observed with a time spacing of typically 1−2 months. In particular, 46 masers out of them have been recognized concerning their periodic flux variation and have light−curve data of stellar visual light. Thus, the present paper shows some statistical views of the observed time variability properties of stellar H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$_2$</tex>O masers. We found a good correlation between a time delay of the variation in the H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$_2$</tex>O maser flux with respect to that in the stellar visual light and the stellar pulsation period. The corresponding phase lags are mildly scattered, but are mainly concentrated in the range, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$0.7\leq\Delta \phi\leq\;$</tex>1.5. We also measured line−of−sight velocity drifts of the individual spectral peaks of H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$_2$</tex>O maser emission, which indicate radial acceleration of mass−loss outflows from the evolved stars. We discuss possible pulsation−driven shock waves that are enhanced near the stellar surface, and are propagating outwards in the circumstellar envelope.

articleTitle: Gravitational Instability of Shocked Interstellar Gas Layers
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: In this paper we investigate gravitational instability of shocked gas layers using linear analysis. An unperturbed state is a self-gravitating isothermal layer which grows with time by the accretion of gas through shock fronts due to a cloud-cloud collision. Since the unperturbed state is not static, and cannot be described by a self-similar solution, we numerically solved the perturbation equations and directly integrated them over time. We took account of the distribution of physical quantities across the thickness. Linearized Rankine-Hugoniot relations were imposed at shock fronts as boundary conditions. The following results are found from our unsteady linear analysis: the perturbation initially evolves in oscillatory mode, and begins to grow at a certain epoch. The wavenumber of the fastest growing mode is given by <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$k=2\sqrt{2\pi G\rho_\mathrm{E} {\cal M\mit}}/c_\mathrm{s}$</tex>, where <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\rho_\mathrm{E},\;c_\mathrm{s}$</tex> and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\cal M\mit$</tex> are the density of the parent clouds, the sound velocity and the Mach number of the collision velocity, respectively. For this mode, the transition epoch from oscillatory to growing mode is given by <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$t_g = 1.2/\sqrt{2\pi G\rho_\mathrm{E} {\cal M\mit}}$</tex>. The epoch at which the fastest growing mode becomes non-linear is given by <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$2.4\delta_0^{-0.1}/\sqrt{2\pi G \rho_\mathrm{E}{\cal M\mit}}$</tex>, where <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\delta_0$</tex> is the initial amplitude of the perturbation of the column density. As an application of our linear analysis, we investigated criteria for collision-induced fragmentation. Collision-induced fragmentation will occur only when parent clouds are cold, or <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha_0=$</tex> 5<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$c_\mathrm{s}^2 R/2G M < 1$</tex>, where <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$R$</tex> and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$M$</tex> are the radius and the mass of parent clouds, respectively.

articleTitle: Stellar Abundances for the Galactic Archeology (SAGA) Database — Compilation of the Characteristics of Known Extremely Metal-Poor Stars
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We describe the construction of a database of extremely metal-poor (EMP) stars in the Galaxy. Our database contains detailed elemental abundances, reported equivalent widths, atmospheric parameters, photometry, and binarity status, compiled from papers in the literature that report on studies of EMP halo stars with [Fe/H]<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\;\le\;$</tex>-2.5. The compilation procedures for this database were designed to assemble data effectively from electronic tables available from online journals. We have also developed a data retrieval system that enables data searches by various criteria and illustrations to explore relationships between stored variables. Currently, our sample includes 1212 unique stars (many of which are studied by more than one group) with more than 15000 individual reported elemental abundances, covering relevant papers published by 2007 December. We discuss the global characteristics of the present database, as revealed by the EMP stars observed to date. For stars with [Fe/H]<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\;\le\;$</tex>-2.5, the number of giants with reported abundances is larger than that of dwarfs by a factor of two. The fraction of carbon-rich stars (among the sample for which the carbon abundance is reported) amounts to <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim\;$</tex>30% for [Fe/H]<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\;\le\;$</tex>-2.5. We find that known binaries exhibit different distributions of the orbital period, according to whether they are giants or dwarfs, and also as a function of the metallicity, although the total sample of such stars is still quite small.

articleTitle: X-Ray Emissions from Three-Dimensional Magnetohydrodynamic Coronal Accretion Flows
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We calculated the radiation spectrum and its time variability of a black-hole accretion disk-corona system based on a three-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulation. In explaining the spectral properties of active galactic nuclei, it is often assumed that they consist of a geometrically thin, optically thick disk and hot, optically thin corona surrounding the thin disk. As for a model of the corona, we adopted the simulation data of three-dimensional, non-radiative MHD accretion flows calculated by Y. Kato and coworkers, while for a thin disk we assumed a standard-type disk. We performed Monte-Carlo radiative transfer simulations of the corona, while taking into account the Compton scattering of soft photons from the thin disk by hot thermal electrons and coronal irradiation heating of the thin disk, which emits blackbody radiation. By adjusting the density parameter of the MHD coronal flow, we could produce emergent spectra that are consistent with those of typical Seyfert galaxies. Moreover, we found rapid time variability in the X-ray emission spectra, originating from a density fluctuation produced by a magnetorotational instability in the MHD corona. The features of reflection component including iron fluorescent line emission are also briefly discussed.

articleTitle: Suzaku Spectroscopy of Extended X-Ray Emission in M17
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present the results of a Suzaku spectroscopic study of soft extended X-ray emission in the HII region of M17. The spectrum of the extended emission was obtained with a high signal-to-noise ratio in a spatially resolved manner using the X-ray Imaging Spectrometer (XIS). We established that contamination by unresolved point sources, the Galactic Ridge X-ray emission, the cosmic X-ray background, and the local hot bubble emission is negligible in the background-subtracted XIS spectrum of the diffuse emission. Half a dozen emission lines were clearly resolved for the first time, including K<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha$</tex> lines of highly ionized O, Ne, and Mg as well as L-series complex of Fe at 0.5-1.5keV. Based on diagnosis of these lines, we obtained the following results: (1) the extended emission is an optically thin thermal plasma, represented well by a single temperature of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex>3.0<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\pm$</tex>0.4MK, (2) the abundances of elements with emission lines in the diffuse spectrum are 0.1-0.3 solar, while those of bright discrete sources are 0.3-1.5 solar, (3) the metal abundances relative to each other in the diffuse emission are consistent with solar, except for a Ne enhancement of a factor of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex>2, (4) both the plasma temperature and the chemical composition of the diffuse emission show no spatial variation across the studied spatial scale of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex>5pc.

articleTitle: Star-Forming Galaxies at z ≈ 0.24 in the Subaru Deep Field and the Sloan Digital Sky Survey
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We made a search for H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha $</tex> emitting galaxies at z<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\approx $</tex> 0.24 in the Subaru Deep Field (SDF) using an archival data set obtained with the Subaru telescope. We carefully selected H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha $</tex> emitters in the narrow-band filter NB816, using <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$B$</tex>, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$V$</tex>, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$R_{\rm C}$</tex>, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$i^\prime$</tex>, and z<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^\prime$</tex> broad-band colors. We obtained a sample of 258 emitting galaxies with observed equivalent widths of (H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha $</tex>+ [NII]6548,6584) greater than 12Å. We also analyzed a sample of H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha $</tex> emitters taken from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) to constrain the luminous end of the H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha $</tex> luminosity function. Using the same selection criteria as those for the SDF, and after excluding AGNs, we obtained 317 H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha $</tex> emitting star-forming galaxies. Combining these two samples of H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha $</tex> emitters found in both SDF and SDSS, we derived an H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha $</tex> luminosity function with best-fit Schechter function parameters of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha $</tex>=-1.31<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{+0.17}_{-0.17}$</tex>, log<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\phi^{*}$</tex>=-2.46<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{+0.34}_{-0.40}$</tex>Mpc<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-3}$</tex>, and log<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$L^{*}$</tex>= 41.99<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{+0.08}_{-0.07}$</tex>ergss<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>. The extinction-corrected H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha $</tex> luminosity density is 4.45<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{+2.96}_{-1.75}$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{39}$</tex>ergss<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>Mpc<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-3}$</tex>. Using the Kennicutt relation between the H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha $</tex> luminosity and star-formation rate, the star-formation rate density in the survey volume was estimated at 0.035<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{+0.024}_{-0.014}M_{\odot}$</tex>yr<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>Mpc<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-3}$</tex>. The angular two-point correlation function of H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha $</tex> emitters over 875 arcmin<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^2$</tex> at z= 0.24 was well-fitted by a power-law form with <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$w(\theta)$</tex>= 0.047<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{+0.017}_{-0.013} \theta^{-0.66 \pm 0.08}$</tex>, corresponding to the correlation function <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\xi(r)$</tex>= [<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$r/$</tex>(2.6<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{+1.0}_{-0.8}$</tex>Mpc)]<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1.66\pm0.08}$</tex>. The small correlation length of H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha $</tex> emitters may imply a weak clustering of active star-forming galaxies.

articleTitle: On Black Hole Mass Estimation from X-Ray Spectra of Ultraluminous X-Ray Sources
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We propose a methodology to derive a black-hole mass for super-critical accretion flow. Here, we use the extended disk blackbody (extended DBB) model, a fitting model in which the effective temperature profile obeys the relation <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$T_{\rm eff} \propto r^{-p}$</tex>, with <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$r$</tex> being the disk radius and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$p$</tex> being treated as a fitting parameter. We first numerically calculate the theoretical flow structure and its spectra for a given black-hole mass, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$M$</tex>, and accretion rate, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\dot{M}$</tex>. Through fitting to the theoretical spectra by the extended DBB model, we can estimate the black-hole mass, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$M_{\rm x}$</tex>, assuming that the innermost disk radius is <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$r_{\rm in}=3r_{\rm g} (\propto M_{\rm x})$</tex>, where <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$r_{\rm g}$</tex> is the Schwarzschild radius. We find, however, that the estimated mass deviates from that adopted in the spectral calculations, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$M$</tex>, even for low-<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\dot{M}$</tex> cases. We also find that the deviations can be eliminated by introducing a new correction for the innermost radius. Using this correction, we calculate mass correction factors, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$M/M_{\rm x}$</tex>, in the super-critical regimes for some sets of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$M$</tex> and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\dot M$</tex>, finding that a mass correction factor ranges between <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$M/M_{\rm x} \sim$</tex>1.2-1.6. The higher is <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\dot{M}$</tex>, the larger does the mass correction factor tend to be. Since the correction is relatively small, we can safely conclude that the black holes in ULXs, which Vierdayanti et al. (2006, PASJ, 58, 915) analyzed, are stellar-mass black holes with the mass being <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$<100M_{\odot}$</tex>.

articleTitle: Suzaku Observations of Hercules X-1: Measurements of the Two Cyclotron Harmonics
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: The accretion-powered pulsar Her X-1 was observed with Suzaku twice in its main-on state, on 2005 October 5-6 and 2006 March 29-30, for a net exposure of 30.5ks and 34.4ks, respectively. In the 2005 and 2006 observations, the source was detected at an average 10-30keV intensity of 290mCrab and 230mCrab, respectively. The intrinsic pulse period was measured on both occasions at 1.23776s by HXD-PIN, after barycentric and binary corrections. The pulse phase-averaged spectra in the energy range above 10keV were well fitted by the “Negative and Positive power-law times EXponential” (NPEX) model, multiplied by a fundamental cyclotron resonance scattering feature at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex>36keV, which appears very significantly in the HXD-PIN data. The resonance profiles were successfully reproduced by a Lorentzian-type scattering cross section, rather than by a Gaussian-type alternative. The pulse phase-averaged HXD-GSO data, covering 50-120keV, are featureless. However, in a differential spectrum between the pulse-decay phase and off-pulse phase, the second-harmonic cyclotron resonance was detected in the GSO data at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex>73keV, with a depth of 1.6<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$_{-0.7}^{+0.9}$</tex>. This makes Her X-1 a 6th pulsar with established second-harmonic resonance. The implications of these results are briefly discussed.

articleTitle: New Photometric Data of Old Open Clusters II. A Dataset for 36 Clusters
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present new photometric data on 36 old open clusters using the 65-cm telescope at Gunma Astronomical Observatory. This dataset is a continuation of photometric data of old open clusters (Hasegawa et al 2004, PASJ, 56, 295) collected mainly in the antigalactic center region. By constructing a color-magnitude diagram, we inspected the main sequence and (if richly populated) red-clump stars to evaluate the cluster parameters, that is, the age, distance, and reddening, by applying an isochrone provided by the Padova group. Now, 49 old clusters have consistently measured parameters (36 clusters in this study and 13 from Hasegawa et al. 2004). The clusters are exclusively older than the Hyades cluster, and the age is distributed in the range 0.6-5.0Gyr. The oldest clusters include Auner 1, Biurakan 12, Berkeley 78, and NGC 2425. Our study includes clusters that are useful in further clarifying the outer disk of the Milky Way, and when inner clusters with galactocentric distances less than 12kpc are compared with outer ones, the latter tends to be less bound to the galactic plane. Nine clusters are found to be cospatial with the northern part of the recently identified stellar overdensity centered in the constellation of Canis Major.

Author Keywords: Galaxy: open clusters and associations: HR diagram

articleTitle: Toward First-Principle Simulations of Galaxy Formation: I. How Should We Choose Star-Formation Criteria in High-Resolution Simulations of Disk Galaxies?
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We performed three-dimensional <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$N$</tex>-body/SPH simulations to study how mass resolution and other model parameters, such as the star-formation efficiency parameter, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$C_*$</tex> and the threshold density for star formation, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$n_{\rm th}$</tex> affect structures of the galactic gaseous/stellar disk. We employed <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$10^6$</tex>–<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$10^7$</tex> particles to resolve a cold (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$T <$</tex> 100 K) and dense (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$n_{\rm H} >$</tex> 100 cm<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-3}$</tex>) phase as well as diffuse, hot phases. We found that structures of the interstellar medium (ISM) and the distribution of young stars were sensitive to the assumed values of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$n_{\rm th}$</tex>. High-<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$n_{\rm th}$</tex> models with <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$n_{\rm th} =$</tex> 100 cm<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-3}$</tex> yielded clumpy multi-phase features in the ISM. Young stars were distributed in a thin disk, of which the half-mass scale height was 10–30 pc. In low-<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$n_{\rm th}$</tex> models with <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$n_{\rm th} =$</tex> 0.1 cm<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-3}$</tex>, which is usually employed in cosmological galaxy-formation simulations, the gas disk appears to be smoother and the stellar disk is found to be several-times thicker than the high-<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$n_{\rm th}$</tex> models. A high-resolution simulation with high-<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$n_{\rm th}$</tex> is necessary to reproduce the complex structure of the gas disk. The global star-formation properties of galaxies, such as the star-formation history, in low-<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$n_{\rm th}$</tex> models are similar to those in high-<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$n_{\rm th}$</tex> models when we tune the value of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$C_*$</tex> so that they reproduce the observed relation between the surface gas density and the surface star-formation rate density. We however emphasize that high-<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$n_{\rm th}$</tex> models automatically reproduce the relation, regardless of the values of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$C_*$</tex>. The ISM structure, phase distribution and distributions of young star-forming regions are quite similar in runs with different values of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$C_*$</tex>. We found that the timescale of the flow from the reservoir (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$n_{\rm H} \sim$</tex> 1 cm<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-3}$</tex> ) to the star-forming regions (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$n_{\rm H} >rsim 100$</tex> cm<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-3}$</tex> ) is about five-times as long as the local dynamical time, and this evolution timescale is independent of the value of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$C_*$</tex>. The use of a high-<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$n_{\rm th}$</tex> criterion for star formation in high-resolution simulations makes numerical models fairy insensitive to the modeling of star formation.

articleTitle: X-Ray Spectroscopy of SN 1006 with Suzaku
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We report on observations of SN 1006 with Suzaku. We firmly detected K-shell emission from Fe, for the first time, and found that the Fe ionization state is quite low. The broad-band spectrum extracted from southeast of the remnant was well-fitted with a model consisting of three optically thin thermal non-equilibrium ionization plasmas and a power-law component. Two of the thermal models are highly overabundant in heavy elements, and hence are likely due to ejecta. These components have different ionization parameters, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$n_{\rm e}t \sim 1.4\times 10^{10}$</tex>cm<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-3}$</tex>s and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$n_{\rm e}t \sim 7.7\times 10^8$</tex>cm<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-3}$</tex>s; it is the later one that produces Fe-K emission. This suggests that Fe has been heated by reverse shock more recently than the other elements, consistent with a picture where the ejecta are stratified by composition with Fe in the interior. On the other hand, the third thermal component is assumed to be solar abundance, and we associate it with emission from the interstellar medium. The electron temperature (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$kT_{\rm e} \sim$</tex>0.5keV) is lower than that expected from the shock velocity, which suggests a lack of collisionless electron heating at the forward shock. The extremely low ionization parameter and extreme non-equilibrium state are due to the low density of the ambient medium.

articleTitle: Suzaku Observation of G359.79-0.26, a New Supernova Remnant Candidate in the Galactic Center
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: Utilizing Suzaku observations, we obtained the X-ray spectrum of G359.79-0.26, an extended X-ray feature nearby the Galactic center (GC) supernova remnant (SNR) SgrA East. We estimated the contribution from the Galactic center diffuse X-rays, which allows us a proper background subtraction from the faint extended source. A thin thermal plasma with a temperature of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$ kT_{\rm e} \sim 1$</tex>keV and slightly enhanced metal abundances (S and Ar) are required to reproduce the G359.79-0.26 spectrum. The absorption column density (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$N_{\rm H} \sim 4 \times 10^{22}$</tex> cm<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-2}$</tex>) associated with the plasma indicates that G359.79-0.26 is located in the GC. The thermal energy of the plasma is estimated to be <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$1.7 \times 10^{50}$</tex>erg, typical for galactic SNRs. Its center-filling X-ray emission surrounded by a shell-like radio structure suggests that G359.79-0.26 would be a new member of the mixed-morphology SNR class. The 2.45keV mosaic image covering a <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 40' \times 40'$</tex> GC field implies an alternative possibility that G359.79-0.26 might be a part of a large ring-like structure with a size of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$18' \times 16'$</tex>.

articleTitle: Catalogue of 12CO(J = 1−0) and 13CO(J = 1−0) Molecular Clouds in the Carina Flare Supershell
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present a catalogue of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{12}$</tex>CO(<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J=$</tex> 1-0) and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{13}$</tex>CO(<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J=$</tex> 1-0) molecular clouds in the spatio-velocity range of the Carina Flare supershell, GSH287+04-17. The data cover a region of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex>66 square degrees and were taken with the NANTEN 4m telescope, at spatial and velocity resolutions of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex>2.6' and 0.1kms<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>. Decomposition of the emission results in the identification of 156 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{12}$</tex>CO clouds and 60 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{13}$</tex>CO clouds, for which we provide observational and physical parameters. Previous work suggests the majority of the detected mass forms part of a comoving molecular cloud complex that is physically associated with the expanding shell. The cloud internal velocity dispersions, degree of virialization and size-linewidth relations are found to be consistent with those of other Galactic samples. However, the vertical distribution is heavily skewed towards high-altitudes. The robust association of high-<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$z$</tex> molecular clouds with a known supershell provides some observational backing for the theory that expanding shells contribute to the support of a high-altitude molecular layer.

articleTitle: Suzaku Observations of the Cluster of Galaxies Abell 2052
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: The results from Suzaku X-ray Imaging Spectrometer (XIS) observations of relaxed cluster of galaxies, Abell 2052, are presented. Offset pointing data were used to estimate the Galactic foreground emission in the direction of the cluster. Significant soft X-ray excess emission above this foreground, the intracluster medium emission, and other background components was confirmed and resolved both radially and spectroscopically. This excess can be described either by (a) local variations of known Galactic emission components or by (b) an additional thermal component with a temperature of about 0.2 keV, possibly associated with the cluster. The radial temperature and metallicity profiles of the intracluster medium were measured within <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim\;$</tex>20<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^\prime$</tex> in radius (about 60% of the virial radius) from the cluster center. The temperature drops radially to 0.5–0.6 of the peak value at a radius of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim\;$</tex>15<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^\prime$</tex>. The gas-mass-weighted metal abundance averaged over the observed region was found to be 0.21<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\;\pm\;$</tex>0.05 times solar.

articleTitle: Clustering of Emission-Line Stars in the W 5 E H II Region
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We have made a new survey of emission-line stars in the W 5 E H II region to investigate the population of PMS stars near the OB stars by using the Wide Field Grism Spectrograph 2 (WFGS2). A total of 139 H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha$</tex> emission stars were detected and their <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$g'i'$</tex>-photometry was performed. Their spatial distribution shows three aggregates, i.e., two aggregates near the bright-rimmed clouds at the edge of the W 5 E H II region (BRC 13 and BRC 14) and one near the exciting O7V star. The age and mass of each H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha$</tex> star were estimated from an extinction–corrected color-magnitude diagram and theoretical evolutionary tracks. We found, for the first time in this region, that the young stars near the exciting star are systematically older (4 Myr) than those near the edge of the H II region (1 Myr). This result supports that the formation of stars proceeds sequentially from the center of H II region to the eastern bright rim. We further suggest a possibility that the birth of low-mass stars near the exciting star of the H II region precedes the production of massive OB stars in the pre-existing molecular cloud.

articleTitle: Discovery of Extended X-Ray Emission from an Unidentified TeV Source, HESS J1614-518, Using the Suzaku Satellite
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We report Suzaku results concerning HESS J1614-518, which is the brightest extended TeV gamma-ray source discovered in the Galactic plane survey conducted using the H.E.S.S. telescope. We discovered three X-ray objects in the field of view of the X-ray Imaging Spectrometer, which were designated as Suzaku J1614-5141 (src A), Suzaku J1614-5152 (src B), and Suzaku J1614-5148 (src C). Src A is an extended source located at the peak position of HESS J1614-518, and is therefore a plausible counterpart to HESS J1614-518. The X-ray flux in the 2-10keV band is 5<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times 10^{-13}$</tex>ergs<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>cm<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-2}$</tex>, which is an order of magnitude smaller than the TeV flux. The photon index is 1.7, which is smaller than the canonical value of synchrotron emissions from high-energy electrons found in some supernova remnants. These findings present a challenge to models in which the origin of TeV emission is inverse Compton scattering of the cosmic microwave background by accelerated electrons that emit X-rays via synchrotron emission. Src B is located at a relatively dim region in the TeV band image; however, its hydrogen column density is the same as that of src A. Therefore, src B may also be physically related to HESS J1614-518. Src C is a foreground late-type B star. We also discovered soft extended X-ray emission near HESS J1614-518.

articleTitle: N2H+ and HC3N Observations of the Orion A Cloud
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: The “<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\int$</tex>-shaped filament” of the Orion A giant molecular cloud was mapped in N<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$_2$</tex>H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^+$</tex>, and its northern end, the OMC-2/3 region, was also observed in HC<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$_3$</tex>N and CCS. The results were compared with maps of other molecular lines and the dust continuum emission. The N<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$_2$</tex>H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^+$</tex> distribution is similar to the dust continuum distribution, except for the central part of the Orion Nebula. The distribution of H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{13}$</tex>CO<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^+$</tex> holds a resemblance to that of the dust continuum, but the N<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$_2$</tex>H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^+$</tex> distribution looks more similar to the dust continuum distribution. The N-bearing molecules, N<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$_2$</tex>H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^+$</tex> and NH<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$_3$</tex>, seem to be more intense in OMC-2, compared with the H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{13}$</tex>CO<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^+$</tex> and CS distribution. This suggests that OMC-2 has a higher abundance of N-bearing molecules, or a higher filling factor of the quiescent gas. We identified 34 cloud cores from N<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$_2$</tex>H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^+$</tex> data. Over the Orion Nebula region, the N<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$_2$</tex>H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^+$</tex> linewidth is large (1.1-2.1kms<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>). In the OMC-2/3 region, it becomes moderate (0.5-1.3kms<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>), and it is smaller (0.3-1.1kms<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>) in the south of the Orion Nebula. On the other hand, the gas kinetic temperature of the quiescent cores observed in N<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$_2$</tex>H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^+$</tex> is rather constant (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex>20K) over the <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\int$</tex>-shaped filament. We detected no CCS emission in the OMC-2/3 region. In general, the N<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$_2$</tex>H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^+$</tex> and HC<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$_3$</tex>N distribution is quite similar in the OMC-2/3 region, but we observed a displacement between N<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$_2$</tex>H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^+$</tex> and HC<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$_3$</tex>N over a 2<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\prime$</tex> scale in OMC-3, which has a chain of Class 0-I protostars (candidates).

Author Keywords: ISM: individual objects (Orion Nebula, Orion Molecular Cloud)

articleTitle: Suzaku Observation of the Anomalous X-Ray Pulsar CXOU J164710.2—455216
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: A Suzaku TOO observation of CXOU J164710.2-455216 was performed on 2006 September 23–24 for a net exposure of 38.8 ks. Pulsations were clearly detected in the XIS light curves with a pulse period of 10.61063(2) s. The XIS pulse profile is found to be highly non-sinusoidal. It shows 3 peaks of different amplitudes with an RMS fractional amplitude of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex>11% in the 0.2–6.0 keV energy band. The 1–10 keV XIS spectra were well fitted by two different models consisting of a power-law and a blackbody component and two blackbody components, respectively. Although both the models are statistically acceptable, a difference in the pulse profiles at soft (0.2–6.0 keV) and hard (6–12 keV) X-rays favors the model consisting of two blackbody components. The temperatures of two blackbody components are found to be 0.61<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\pm$</tex>0.01 keV and 1.22<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\pm$</tex>0.06 keV, and the value of the absorption column density is 1.73<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\pm$</tex>0.03 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex> 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{22}$</tex>atoms cm<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-2}$</tex>. Pulse phase resolved spectroscopy shows that the flux of the soft blackbody component consists of three narrow peaks, whereas the flux of the other component shows a single peak over the pulse period of the AXP. The blackbody radii change between 2.2–2.7 km and 0.28–0.38 km (assuming the source distance to be 5 kpc) over the pulse phases for the soft and hard components, respectively. The details of the results obtained from the timing and spectral analyses are presented.

articleTitle: Aligned Molecular Clouds towards SS 433 and L = 348$^{\circ}$5: Possible Evidence for a Galactic “Vapor Trail” Created by a Relativistic Jet
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We carried out a detailed analysis of the NANTEN <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{12}$</tex>CO (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J=$</tex> 1–0) dataset in two large areas towards SS 433 (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$l \sim$</tex> 40<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^\circ$</tex>) and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$l \sim$</tex> 348<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{\circ}$</tex>5. In SS 433, we detected ten clouds, which are well aligned nearly along the axis of an X-ray jet emanating from SS 433 at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$V_{\rm LSR}$</tex> = 42–56 km s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>. The total length of the feature is <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim\;$</tex>300 pc, three-times longer than that of the X-ray jet, at 3 kpc. Towards <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$l \sim$</tex>348<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{\circ}$</tex>5, we detected four aligned clouds at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$V_{\rm LSR}$</tex> = -80–-100 km s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>, nearly perpendicular to the Galactic plane. The total length of the feature is <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim\;$</tex>400 pc at 6 kpc. In both cases, the CO clouds are distributed at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mid{b}\mid\;\sim$</tex> 1<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${}^\circ$</tex>–5<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">${}^\circ$</tex> and their alignments and coincidence in velocity should be rare, suggesting that they are physically associated. We present a scenario to explain these aligned clouds in which the interaction between a relativistic jet and the interstellar medium induced molecular cloud formation over the last <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim\;$</tex>10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{5\hbox{--}6}$</tex>yr. It is suggested that the timescale of the relativistic jet may be considerably larger, on the order of 10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{5\hbox{--}6}$</tex>yr, than previously thought in SS 433. The driving engine of the jet is obviously SS 433, itself, in SS 433, although the engine is not yet identified in <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$l \sim$</tex>348<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{\circ}$</tex>5 among possible several candidates detected in X-rays and TeV gamma rays.

articleTitle: Non-Thermal Spectra from Pulsar Magnetospheres in the Full Electromagnetic Cascade Scenario
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We simulated non-thermal emission from a pulsar magnetosphere within the framework of a full polar-cap cascade scenario by taking the acceleration gap into account, using the Monte Carlo method. For a given electric field parallel to open field lines located at some height above the surface of a neutron star, primary electrons were accelerated by parallel electric fields and lost their energies by curvature radiation; these photons were converted to electron–positron pairs, which emitted photons through subsequent quantum synchrotron radiation and inverse Compton scattering, leading to a cascade. In our calculations, the acceleration gap was assumed to be high above the stellar surface (about several stellar radii); the primary and secondary particles and photons emitted during the journey of those particles in the magnetosphere were traced using the Monte Carlo method. In such a scenario, we calculated the non-thermal photon spectra for different pulsar parameters and compared the model results for two normal pulsars and one millisecond pulsar with the observed data.

articleTitle: Spectral Study of the Galactic Ridge X-Ray Emission with Suzaku
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: In order to carry out a precise spectral study of the Galactic Ridge X-ray Emission using Suzaku, we have observed a typical Galactic plane field at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$(l,b) =$</tex> (28D46, -0D20), which is already deeply observed with Chandra, and known to be devoid of bright X-ray point sources. Thanks to the low background and high spectral resolution of Suzaku, we were able to resolve three narrow iron K-emission lines from low-ionized (6.41keV), helium-like (6.67keV), and hydrogenic ions (7.00keV). The cosmic-ray ion charge-exchange model or the non-equilibrium ionization plasma model are unlikely to explain these line features, since they require either broad emission lines or lines at intermediate ionization states. Collisional ionization equilibrium plasma is the likely origin for the 6.67keV and 7.00keV lines; however, the origin of the 6.41keV line, which is due to fluorescence from cold material, has not been elucidated. We could also precisely measure the absolute X-ray surface brightness in the direction of the Galactic plane. Excluding point sources brighter than <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex>2 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times 10^{-13}$</tex>ergs<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>cm<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-2}$</tex> (2-10keV), the total surface brightness on the Galactic plane is <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex>6.1 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times 10^{-11}$</tex>ergs<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>cm<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-2}$</tex>deg<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-2}$</tex> (2-10keV), including the contribution of the cosmic X-ray background, which is estimated to be <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex>1.3<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times 10^{-11}$</tex>ergs<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>cm<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-2}$</tex>deg<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-2}$</tex>.

articleTitle: Performance of an Imaging Fourier Transform Spectrometer with Photoconductive Detector Arrays: An Application for the AKARI Far-Infrared Instrument
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We have developed an imaging Fourier transform spectrometer (FTS) for space-based far-infrared astronomical observations. The FTS employs newly developed photoconductive detector arrays with a capacitive trans-impedance amplifier, which makes the FTS a completely unique instrument. The FTS was installed as a function of the far-infrared instrument (FIS: Far-Infrared Surveyor) aboard the Japanese astronomical satellite, AKARI, which was launched on 2006 February 21 (UT) from Uchinoura Space Center. The FIS-FTS had been operated for more than one year before liquid helium ran out on 2007 August 26. The FIS-FTS was operated nearly six hundreds times, which corresponds to more than one hundred hours of astronomical observations and almost the same amount of time for calibrations. As expected from laboratory measurements, the FIS-FTS performed well and has produced a large set of astronomical data for valuable objects. Meanwhile, it has become clear that the detector transient effect is a considerable factor for FTSs with photoconductive detectors. In this paper, the instrumentation of the FIS-FTS and interesting phenomena related to FTS using photoconductive detectors are described, and future applications of this kind of FTS system are discussed.

articleTitle: Astrometry of H2O Masers in Nearby Star-Forming Regions with VERA III. IRAS22198+6336 in Lynds1204G
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present results of multi-epoch VLBI observations with VERA (VLBI Exploration of Radio Astrometry) of the 22GHz H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$_{2}$</tex>O masers associated with a young stellar object (YSO) IRAS22198+6336 in a dark cloud, L1204G. Based on phase-referencing VLBI astrometry, we derived an annual parallax of IRAS22198+6336 to be 1.309<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\pm$</tex>0.047mas, corresponding to the distance of 764<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\pm$</tex>27pc from the Sun. Although the most principal error source of our astrometry is attributed to the internal structure of the maser spots, we successfully reduced the errors in the derived annual parallax by employing position measurements for all of the 26 detected maser spots. Based on this result, we reanalyzed the spectral energy distribution of IRAS22198+6336 and found that the bolometric luminosity and total mass of IRAS22198+6336 are 450<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$L_{\odot}$</tex> and 7<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$M_{\odot}$</tex>, respectively. These values are consistent with an intermediate-mass YSO deeply embedded in the dense dust core, which has been proposed to be an intermediate-mass counterpart of a low-mass Class 0 source. In addition, we obtained absolute proper motions of the H<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$_{2}$</tex>O masers for the most blue-shifted components. We propose that the collimated jets aligned along the east-west direction are the most plausible explanation for the origin of the detected maser features.

articleTitle: Role of Compressibility, Turbulent Viscosity, and Mass-Transfer-Rate on Accretion Discs in Close Binaries
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: In this work, the roles of both the inflow kinematic conditions at the inner Lagrangian point L1 as an initial boundary condition and the gas compressibility, physical turbulent viscosity on an accretion disc’s dynamics and structure were investigated via simulations of 3D SPH stationary accretion-disc models. Physical viscosity supports accretion-disc development inside the primary gravitational potential well in a close binary system, even for low-compressibility modelling. Currently, an assigned typical turbulent Shakura-Sunyaev parameter, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha \simeq 0.1$</tex>, is widely adopted for these structures. Such an investigation was carried out here with the aim of evaluating, in a compressibility-viscosity graph, the most suitable domains where the physical conditions allow a well-bound disc development as a function of the mass-transfer kinematic conditions. Physical, turbulent viscosity is represented by a viscous force contribution, expressed by the divergence of the symmetric viscous stress tensor in the Navier-Stokes equation, while the viscous energy contribution is given by a symmetric combination of the symmetric shear tensor multiplied by the particle velocity. The same binary system parameters-stellar masses and their separation–were adopted throughout, whilst the adopted polytropic index, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\gamma$</tex>, is chosen to be in the range between 1-(5/3). The results show that in such domains, the lower is the gas compressibility (the higher the polytropic index <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\gamma$</tex>), the higher is the physical viscosity (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha$</tex>) requested. Conclusions, as far as dwarf nova outbursts are concerned, induced by mass-transfer rate variations are also reported.

Author Keywords: stars: binaries: close, dwarf novae, cataclysmic variables

articleTitle: Discovery of a Bright Transient Ultraluminous X-Ray Source, Suzaku J1305–4931 in NGC4945
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: An X-ray source, Suzaku J1305-4931, was discovered in the south-west arm of a nearby Seyfert II galaxy, NGC4945, at 0.5-10keV flux of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$2.2 \times 10^{-12}$</tex>ergcm<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-2}$</tex>s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex> during a Suzaku observation conducted on 2006 January 15-17. It was undetectable in a shorter observation on 2005 August 22-23, with an upper limit of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$1.7 \times 10^{-14}$</tex>ergcm<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-2}$</tex>s<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>. At a distance of 3.7Mpc, the bolometric luminosity of the source became <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$L_{\rm bol} = 4.4 \times 10^{39} \alpha$</tex>ergs<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>, where <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha = ({\rm\cos} 60^\circ \!/ \cos i)$</tex> and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$i$</tex> is the disk inclination. The time-averaged X-ray spectrum of the source is described by a multi-color disk model, with an innermost disk temperature of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$T_{\rm in} = 1.69_{-0.05}^{+0.06}$</tex>keV. It varied by a factor of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$2$</tex> in intensity, following a clear correlation of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$L_{\rm bol} \propto T_{\rm in}^4$</tex>. The innermost disk radius is inferred to stay constant at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$R_{\rm in} = 79_{-3.9}^{+4.0} \alpha^{1/2}$</tex> km, suggesting the presence of a standard accretion disk. Relating <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$R_{\rm in}$</tex> with the last stable orbit around a non-rotating black hole yields a rather low black-hole mass, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 9 \alpha^{1/2}$</tex> solar masses, which would imply that the source is shining at a considerable super-Eddington luminosity. These results can be better interpreted by invoking sub-Eddington emission from a rapidly spinning black hole with 20-130 solar masses.

articleTitle: Wide-Band Spectroscopy of the Compton Thick Seyfert2 Galaxy Markarian 3 with Suzaku
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We obtained a wide-band spectrum of the Compton-thick Seyfert2 galaxy Mkn3 with Suzaku. The observed spectrum was clearly resolved into weak, soft power-law emission, a heavily absorbed power-law component, cold reflection, and many emission lines. The heavily absorbed component, absorbed by gas with a column density of 1.1<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex>10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{24}$</tex>cm<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-2}$</tex>, has an intrinsic 2-10keV luminosity of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim$</tex>1.6<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex>10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{43}$</tex>ergs<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>, and is considered to be direct emission from the Mkn3 nucleus. The reflection component was interpreted as being the reflection of direct light off a cold, thick material; the reflection fraction, <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$R$</tex>, was 1.36<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\pm$</tex>0.20. The cold material is inferred to be located <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$>$</tex> 1 pc from the central black hole of Mkn3, due to the low ionization parameter of iron (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\xi <$</tex> 1ergcms<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>) and the narrow iron line width (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sigma$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$<$</tex> 22eV). The weak, soft power-law emission is considered to be scattered light by ionized gas with a scattering fraction of 0.9<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\pm$</tex>0.2%. The existence of many highly ionized lines in the observed spectrum indicates that the ionized gas has a broad ionized structure, with <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\xi =$</tex> 10-1000 ergcms<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex>. This high-quality spectrum obtained by Suzaku can be considered to be a template for studies of Seyfert2 galaxies.

articleTitle: AKARI/FIS Mapping of the ISM-Wind Bow Shock around $\alpha $ Orionis
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$10$</tex><tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\times$</tex>50scan maps around an M supergiant <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha $</tex> Ori at 65, 90, 140, and 160<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mu$</tex>m obtained with the AKARI Infrared Astronomy Satellite. Higher spatial resolution data with the exact analytic solution permit us to fit the de-projected shape of the stellar-wind bow shock around <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha $</tex> Ori to have a stand-off distance of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$4\frac{m}{8}$</tex>, position angle of 55<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{\circ}$</tex> and inclination angle of 56<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{\circ}$</tex>. The shape of the bow shock suggests that the velocity of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha $</tex> Ori with respect to the local medium is <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$v_* = 40n_{\rm H}^{-1/2}$</tex>, where <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$n_{\rm H}$</tex> is the hydrogen nucleus density at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha $</tex> Ori. We found that the local medium is of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$n_{\rm H} =$</tex> 1.5 to 1.9cm<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-3}\rule[3mm]{0mm}{0mm}$</tex> and the velocity of the local flow is at 11kms<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$^{-1}$</tex> by using the most recent astrometric solutions for <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha $</tex> Ori under the assumption that the medium local to <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\alpha $</tex> Ori is moving away from the Orion OB 1 association. AKARI images may also reveal a vortex ring due to instabilities on the surface of the bow shock, as demonstrated by numerical models. This research exemplifies the potential of AKARI All-Sky data as well as follow-up observations with Herschel Space Telescope and Stratospheric Observatory for Infrared Astronomy for this avenue of research in revealing the nature of the interaction between the stellar wind and the interstellar medium.

articleTitle: SiO Maser Observations toward Orion-KL with VERA
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present results of phase-referencing VLBI observations of SiO masers in the Orion-KL region made with VERA. Using a strong maser spot in the 43GHz <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$v =$</tex> 2 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J=$</tex> 1-0 emission, we derived the trigonometric parallax of Orion-KL to be 2.39<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\pm$</tex>0.03mas, corresponding to a distance of 418<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\pm$</tex>6pc, with the highest accuracy among existing parallax measurements of the source. We made a superimposed image of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$v =$</tex> 1 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J=$</tex> 1-0 and <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$v =$</tex> 2 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$J=$</tex> 1-0 maser features in Orion-KL based on absolute positions obtained from the phase-referencing astrometry with a common reference source. The maser features of both transitions show similar X-shaped distributions centered at Source I. However, in each of the four arms of the X-shape, the SiO <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$v =$</tex> 2 features tend to lie closer to Source I than the SiO <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$v =$</tex> 1 features. The radial velocities of the maser emission decrease with the distance from Source I. The spatial and radial velocity distributions of the SiO masers suggest that the SiO masers lie in the rotating materials associated with a disk around Source I, rather than a decelerating outflow.

articleTitle: Supernova Remnants in the AKARI IRC Survey of the Large Magellanic Cloud
publicationTitle: Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
abstract: We present a near- to mid-infared study of supernova remnants (SNRs) using the AKARI IRC Survey of the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC). The LMC survey observed about a 10 square degree area of the LMC in five bands centered at 3, 7, 11, 15, and 24<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mu$</tex>m using the Infrared Camera (IRC) aboard AKARI. The number of SNRs in the survey area is 21, which is about a half of the known LMC SNRs. We systematically examined AKARI images and identified eight SNRs with distinguishable infrared emission. All of them were detected at <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$>rsim$</tex>10<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mu$</tex>m and some at 3 and 7<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mu$</tex>m, too. We present their AKARI images and fluxes. In the 11/15<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mu$</tex>m versus 15/24<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mu$</tex>m color-color diagram, the SNRs appear to be aligned along a modified blackbody curve, representing thermal emission from dust at temperatures of between 90 and 190K. There is a good correlation between the 24<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mu$</tex>m and X-ray fluxes of the SNRs. It was also found that there is a good correlation between the 24<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\mu$</tex>m and radio fluxes even if there is no direct physical connection between them. We considered the origin of the detected mid-infrared emission in individual SNRs.
